name: Interactive Media System
definition: The use of digital technologies to present combinations of text, graphics, video, animation and/or sound in an integrated way that the user can interact with.
example: An interactive game, a media-rich website or an e-book.

name: User Interface (UI)
definition: The means by which users interact with computer hardware or software, such as fields, buttons and pointers in software, or switches and dials in hardware.
example: The buttons, menus and text fields on a school canteen ordering page.

name: Assets
definition: The digital elements that can be used in a multimedia production, including graphics, photographs, video, audio and animations.
example: A logo in SVG, a photo in JPEG and an interview in MP4 used on one website.

name: Data Compression
definition: A reduction in the number of bits needed to represent data, saving storage and transmission time.
example: Saving a photo as a JPEG so it downloads faster.

name: Lossless Compression
definition: Compression that keeps enough information to rebuild the original data exactly.
example: A PNG screenshot or a FLAC audio file.

name: Lossy Compression
definition: Compression that permanently discards information unlikely to be noticed, so the original cannot be restored.
example: An MP3 or a JPEG at low quality that shows blocky artefacts.

name: Sampling Rate
definition: The number of times per second a sound wave is measured when it is digitised.
example: CD audio uses 44,100 samples per second.

name: Bit Depth
definition: The number of bits used to record each sample or pixel, which sets how many different values can be stored.
example: 16-bit audio allows 65,536 possible heights per sample; 24-bit colour allows about 16.7 million colours.

name: Wireframe
definition: A simple, low-fidelity layout of a screen that shows structure and placement without colour or final content.
example: Grey boxes labelled Header, Image and Button on a sketch of a home page.

name: Storyboard
definition: A diagram showing the screens of an interface and the links between them; in NESA notation, buttons with a dot and arrow show which screen they open.
example: Three linked screens for a school canteen website: Home, Prices and Specials.

name: Prototype
definition: A trial product or model built to test an idea and inform further design, which can be physical or digital.
example: A clickable model of an ordering screen tested with five students.

name: Design Thinking
definition: A process of identifying a need and developing a design solution, considering economic, environmental and social impacts, using empathise, define, ideate, prototype and test.
example: Interviewing students about lunch queues, then testing a paper prototype of an ordering site.

name: Nudging (Guided Choice)
definition: A design choice that steers people towards an option without removing other options.
example: A "Most popular" badge on one product or a pre-selected delivery option.

name: Dark Pattern
definition: A deceptive design technique that steers users into choices that are not in their interest.
example: A cancel link hidden behind five clicks while sign-up takes one.

name: Cookie
definition: A small piece of data a website stores in the browser to keep a session, remember preferences or track activity.
example: A shopping cart that remembers items after you close the tab.

name: Digital Footprint
definition: The traces of data left behind by a person using a digital system, both actively given and passively collected.
example: Posts you share (active) and your IP address in server logs (passive).

name: Auto-profiling
definition: The automatic building of a picture of a person by inferring interests and characteristics from their behaviour without them entering it.
example: A video app recommending content based on what you watched, not on what you said you liked.

name: Creative Commons
definition: A non-profit organisation whose standard licences let creators share work while stating how others may reuse it.
example: A photo licensed CC BY 4.0 that you can reuse if you credit the creator.

name: Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property (ICIP)
definition: The rights of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples in their cultural heritage, including knowledge, art, stories, languages and designs.
example: Asking the relevant community for permission before using traditional artwork on a website.

name: Crowdsourcing
definition: Using a large group of people, usually online, to contribute information, ideas or work.
example: Residents reporting flood levels through a community social media page.

name: Massive Open Online Course (MOOC)
definition: An online course open to very large numbers of learners, often free to start.
example: A free university course delivered by video, quizzes and forums.

name: Massive Multiplayer Online Game (MMOG)
definition: An online game in which very large numbers of players share one persistent world.
example: Guilds of players completing a shared quest in a persistent online world.

name: Sandbox Gaming
definition: A virtual world where players build their own playscapes, invite others to play and test game play.
example: Building and sharing a mini-game in Minecraft.

name: Data Journalism
definition: Finding, analysing and presenting data to tell a news story, often using interactive charts or maps.
example: An interactive map letting readers look up rainfall in their own town.

name: Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG)
definition: The W3C's internationally recognised guidelines for making web content accessible, organised under four principles: perceivable, operable, understandable and robust.
example: Providing alt text for images and at least 4.5:1 contrast for body text.
